idiom_name: spool file: write + fsync + rename, unlink only after the peer's ack
implementation_notes: libc offers no durable messaging primitive, so the classic structure is hand-written around the filesystem: write the frame to a temporary file in a per-destination spool directory, fsync() the file, rename() it to its final name and fsync() the directory so the rename is durable too; only then transmit, and unlink the file only after the peer acknowledged. At start-up a recovery pass replays every spool entry that is still present, and the peer deduplicates on the message id carried in the frame. The hand-written form is the only form: POSIX message queues (mq_send) are kernel objects with a fixed depth that do not survive a reboot, so they can be a transport but never the store. Introduce a real client library (librdkafka, librabbitmq, nanomsg) as soon as the guarantee must span hosts or the spool logic starts to grow business rules.
pitfalls: fsync() on the file is not enough: without a second fsync() on the directory the rename can be lost in a crash, so the message disappears although the data blocks were written.
write() may be short and fsync() reports deferred I/O errors (EIO, ENOSPC) only when it is called - ignoring either return value loses data silently.
POSIX message queues (mq_send) are not persistent across reboot and have a bounded queue depth; blocking mq_send with O_NONBLOCK unset can stall the sender thread indefinitely.
Never unlink on 'write returned' - the unlink must be gated on the peer's acknowledgement, and the recovering process must be the same code path that sends.
